newsitem.title: USA: Crew boards for U.S. space shuttle launch.
newsitem.headline: Crew boards for U.S. space shuttle launch.

text.p: Six astronauts climbed aboard the space shuttle Discovery on Thursday for mid-morning launch on a mission packed with scientific objectives.
The shuttle crew, wearing bright orange pressure suits, were strapped into their cockpit seats about two hours before the planned blast-off.
Discovery was scheduled to roar off its launch pad at Florida's Kennedy Space Centre at 10:41 a.m. EDT (1441 GMT), weather permitting.

Early Thursday morning, launch controllers completed the three-hour operation to load the shuttle's giant strap-on fuel tank with a half million gallons of supercold liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen propellants.
Forecasters said there was a 40 percent chance that bad weather associated with a rare mid-summer cold front would delay Discovery's launch.
"Our primary concern is for the potential for some showers popping up in and around the area," U.S. Air Force meteorologist Scott Jacobs said.
Aboard the shuttle are mission commander Curt Brown, co-pilot Kent Rominger, mission specialists Jan Davis, Robert Curbeam and Stephen Robinson and Canadian researcher Bjarni Tryggvason.

During their 11-day mission, the astronauts were to study the Earth's protective ozone layer, point a telescope at Comet Hale-Bopp and test a Japanese robot arm intended for use on the international space station.
Other tasks include monitoring vegetation on Earth, growing colon cancer cells for medical research and testing positioning systems for constructing the space station.
"It's a very interesting flight," shuttle programme manager Tommy Holloway said. "We have something for everyone."
